blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Yes, Mr Astbury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, I call Dr Elizabeth Newby, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR ELIZABETH NEWBY (affirmed)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Good morning. Can we start with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Elizabeth Anne Newby.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And your profession, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Doctor.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Thank you. We understand that you were employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital, certainly during the month of June of 2015, in (inaudible) capacity as a consultant; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Can I begin by asking when you first qualified as a doctor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Gosh. 1995.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And qualified in your specialty?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I finished my training in 2006.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And your specialty is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Paediatrics.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Thank you. You were employed at Chester in the capacity of a consultant paediatrician?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: When did you start at Chester as a consultant?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... Beginning of 2006. Sort of February/March time, I think.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So you'd been there some years at the time I'm going to ask you some questions about now in June 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We've heard about the general set-up with consultants at the time, for example the consultant of the week system, weekend cover and night cover. Did you have any additional responsibilities when you were at Chester at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not particularly, no.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you questions, please, about a baby called [Baby D], who we know was born just after 4 o'clock on 20 June 2015, which was a Saturday --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: -- by emergency caesarean section at an age of 37 plus 1, as it's expressed, as far as her gestation was concerned. She had a history of premature rupture of membranes. We have heard from other junior doctors who treated [Baby D] and her condition and treatment through her period on the neonatal unit. I'm going to ask you please about your contact with [Baby D]. You may be asked more about those details in due course but I'm going to ask you about your contact. There will be notes, hopefully, appearing on the screen to assist you as we go through.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Good, okay.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: My understanding is your first dealings with [Baby D] were on the evening of 20 June 2015, so that would have been later in the day she was born. We've heard she was admitted to the NNU some hours after her birth.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could you from recollection, initially, tell us, please, how you came to deal with [Baby D] on that particular evening?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could I see the medical notes?
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Of course, yes. Could I ask Mr Murphy to go to slide 34. What you'll see is we have a coloured presentation, but behind the slides we'll go to the original notes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay, thank you.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Hopefully that helps. Slide 34, please. These are notes from Dr Brunton, but I understand that at that stage you had a conversation with him about [Baby D]; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So if we go to his notes. They're timed at 21.45.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Cast your eye over those notes, please. Are you able -they do continue on to the next page. If we could briefly go on to the next page if that helps.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's fine, thank you.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So having refreshed your memory from those, do you recall any contact with Dr Brunton that evening concerning [Baby D]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Yes, Dr Brunton had phoned me at home. I had left the unit for the day, but I was aware of [Baby D] because Dr Rylance had made me aware of her and Dr Brunton telephoned me to say that he felt that she wasn't managing on CPAP, her gases had deteriorated, and so he wished -- he felt that the right course of action was to intubate and ventilate her and I agreed with that and he went ahead and did that.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: I mentioned earlier this was a Saturday --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: -- and you described you were on the unit earlier but you'd gone home. So what were your responsibilities over that particular weekend?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So as the consultant on call, we would always be in the hospital from 9 in the morning to complete ward rounds, so to see every patient that was admitted, that was on the ward, on the paediatric ward and on the neonatal unit, and then we would stay until it was -- things had quietened down, everything was sorted and there were no outstanding issues or particularly sick patients that needed review, and then we would be on call from home.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. I mentioned before this was a Saturday.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Would you do just the Saturday or both days of the weekend?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Both days.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So you discussed with Dr Brunton intubating [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: You presumably had an input into the decision?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We've seen and heard that that was then what took place.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: You have helpfully set out -- I'm just going to ask you to cast your eye again over those notes. They run across two pages. If we can go back to the first page, please, and if you can just take a moment and tell us, please, if there's anything significant in there that you recall informing your decision or that stands out to you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So she was requiring a relatively high percentage of oxygen. On the CPAP she was needing 48% oxygen, and she had a respiratory acidosis shown on her blood gas, which means that she is not managing to clear CO2 effectively --
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: That's carbon dioxide --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: -- exhaled by the body and that has an effect on the -is that the pH of the blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So yes, so she has a respiratory acidosis, a high carbon dioxide, and a high oxygen requirement and at the time in 2015 CPAP was what was available to us as a non-invasive mode of helping babies with their ventilation. So at that time the next step would be intubation and ventilation.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And we've heard that that involves passing a tube down the baby's throat --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: -- and into the lungs to assist with breathing.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. Again, if we can go to the second page, please, and check there's nothing else there that significantly bore on your decision or your discussions at that stage.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. That's fine.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Thank you. Now, after intubation has been facilitated, I understand the process is to take an X-ray of the baby to check the position of the tube.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So if we could go next, please, to slide number 3 and go behind it. Would you have been alert to this or would this have been Dr Brunton's sole responsibility to review this?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Brunton would have reviewed this, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So if we can go, please, to slide 50. Scroll down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see what we've been told is effectively a sticker which goes into the notes and which deals with the findings of any given X-ray or scan or imaging that takes place. Is that in accordance with your understanding?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go next, please, to -- is there anything -- I mean you've seen -- you've been through the notes
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: in preparing your statement. Is there anything of note in respect of the position of the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As Dr Brunton's commented, it's a little bit high, the tube, it's sat just at her clavicles, so he has advanced that a little bit, by 0.75 of a centimetre, and has documented that he has done that, which would be -- would make the tube more secure.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Could we go next, please, to slide 55, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see that the slide at the front had your name on, so I'm going to ask you, please, to look at the document that's behind it and explain to us what that pathology report tells us. That was taken, as I understand it, later in that particular evening.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So [Baby D] had been noted to have a raised bilirubin level when she was first admitted to the unit, which was higher than expected for her age at that time.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So we would investigate to look for an underlying cause of that. One of the underlying causes for that would be a discrepancy between the maternal and the baby's blood group. The most common cause would be, for example, a Rhesus negative mum and a Rhesus positive baby or an ABO incompatibility. This showed that the baby's blood group was A positive and there were no antibodies detected in the baby's blood which shows that there was no blood group incompatibility, so that was very unlikely to be the cause for the raised bilirubin.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So that's to do with that bilirubin level, which we have heard referred to -- well, relating to jaundice and discolouration of the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Slide 107, next, please. I understand your next involvement with [Baby D] was the following morning, the morning of the 21st, which is now the Sunday.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: I'm going to ask to go to your notes, please. If you could explain to us -- we can see there 9.25 that morning.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Your name at the top. Is that "D2"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Day 2 of life it refers to, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Thank you. Then [Baby D]'s age on the next line; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: "37 plus 1 weeks' gestation. Caesarean section for failed induction."
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So I've just recapped the history a little bit from the day before.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Take us through that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It says that:
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: "[She was] born in good condition but had an apnoeic episode reported at 12 minutes of age."
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Ie she's stopped breathing:
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: "She then started grunting after that. She was brought round to the neonatal unit at 3.5 hours of age, was noted to be cyanosed with poor saturations in the 40s."
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Pausing there, cyanosed is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: To appear blue.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right. That's a sign of what?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Poor oxygenation.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right. And that would be presumably consistent with the saturation figure that you have then gone on to mention which represents what, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the percentage of oxygen in the blood, if you like.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So it's in the 40s, where would you expect or hope to have it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Hopefully over 92 for a baby of that gestation.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. And then your next note confirms what you told us, she was initially on CPAP?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: But then as a consequence of your conversation with Dr Brunton, ventilated overnight?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Could you then take us, please, through the rest of your note, which can I confirm is based on your examination --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: -- of [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Dr Brunton had extubated her just prior to handover at 9 o'clock because she had done extremely well on the ventilator and very quickly after being extubated her gases had normalised and the oxygen levels had come down, probably in relation to having received a dose of surfactant, which is a drug that we give to help with the compliance of the lungs, which we give down the ET tube when we intubate and ventilate babies.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: So actually, prior to handover in the morning, she had been very good on minimal pressures and low oxygen, so he had extubated her for review on the ward round. And indeed she seemed good from a respiratory point of view.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: She'd been extubated 25 minutes prior to my review, she was self-ventilating in air --
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Pausing there, that's obviously SVIA. Does that mean any breathing assistance at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. So she was breathing on her own, yes, in air, so no supplementary oxygen. Her saturations were 100% in air.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: She was pink and well perfused. I felt that she was a bit quiet still and so I had noted that heart sounds were normal, her chest was clear, I felt that when I examined her, when I handled her and moved her limbs, she felt perhaps slightly as if her tone was a little bit increased.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Explain to us tone, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tone. So your tone is -- gosh, how can I explain tone?
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: I hope you can!
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So rather than feel it -- so if you have low tone you'll be floppy, so you won't be able to maintain and hold your posture, if you like. If you picked up a floppy baby it would
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: almost sort of hang in your arms like a rag doll, is the best way to explain it.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: A slightly -- a baby with slightly increased tone, when you moved their limbs they might not move as fluidly as you expected, you might feel some resistance to movement.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right. So here, tone was increased, so was that the latter of the scenarios?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. She felt a little bit tense and stiff to handle.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. Then the last line in that paragraph, if I can put it that way, something present?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Moro. The Moro reflex is a primitive reflex that babies have. If you hold them and then you slightly let their head go, there is a natural reflex that they will push their --
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right. For the benefit of the tape, you're holding your hands up and throwing them up as if -- does the baby not quite jolt but react?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's a primitive reflex.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And in respect of your examination of [Baby D], what, if anything, did that tell you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was normal, so I was a little bit more reassured about her neurological examination.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. Then P stands for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Plan.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Could you tell us please what the plan was based on your examination that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So we'd recently extubated her, so we needed to do a capillary gas an hour post extubation to confirm she was managing off the ventilator, continue with the IV antibiotics, repeat her U&Es, which refer to blood electrolytes and renal function, because she was on IV fluids, we weren't feeding her at that point. And CRP refers to C-reactive protein, which is a non-specific inflammatory marker, which is -- when raised can be indicative of infection.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And await the blood cultures, which is blood that we always take when we -- before starting babies on antibiotics to see if there are any organisms in the blood that we could identify responsible for infection.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Did you have any particular concern at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I felt it was likely that there was an element of infection given the history. We knew that she had -- mum had had prolonged rupture of membranes, she'd had the apnoeic episode just shortly after birth. She had developed respiratory distress and needed intubating, slightly increased tone, and the fact that she was a bit quiet would all be consistent with infection.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. I understand that the next time you had any involvement with [Baby D] was when you received a call from Dr Rylance; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: That was 1 o'clock that afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: I think if we can go, please, to slide 127. If we click into that. I know it says Dr Chowdhury. That's the same page. If we go down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see there a note at 13.25 --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: -- shortly after your conversation with Dr Rylance.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Does that assist with the conversation that you had with her?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Yes, Dr Rylance had phoned me to say that although, from a respiratory point of view, [Baby D] appeared to be doing well, she was concerned that she remained quite quiet and I think -- I'm trying to...
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: I think there was a blood gas that had a bit of a metabolic component, so she'd wanted to give her a little bit of fluid and she felt that we should have some central access so that we could monitor the situation a bit more clearly.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: I'll ask you to pause there. Metabolic component?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So a blood gas looks at respiratory status and also a metabolic component, which would be a surrogate measure for your cardiovascular status. So a metabolic acidosis implies that you're not perfusing your tissues as well as you should be and therefore you're building up lactic acid, which would give you the acidosis. So yes, a metabolic acidosis would imply some kind
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: of cardiovascular compromise and underperfusion of peripheral tissues.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Perfusion being?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The amount of blood and oxygen that's getting to the tissues.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Thank you. As a result of your conversation was any decision made?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the decision was -- Dr Rylance wanted to insert some umbilical lines to give us a little bit more of a clearer picture of what was going on so I agreed that that was a very reasonable thing to do. I think, although I don't know if it's — I'd have to refer to the notes whether it was documented, but I think she gave [Baby D] some fluid and actually, after insertion of the lines, the gases were better and things seemed to improve.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We can see from the note that those -- well, tell us what the note tells us, please. It says UVC and UAC.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: "UVC inserted, SPR Rylance, aseptic technique, at 5 centimetres. UAC inserted, SPR Rylance, aseptic technique at 20.5 centimetres."
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And those are the batch numbers for the lines that went in.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. If we can go, please, to slide 133. We can see there the note timed at 2 o'clock from Dr Rylance.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So yes, Dr Rylance has attempted to insert the lines. Unfortunately, she wasn't able to advance the UVC far enough, so that was removed. So she had continued and inserted the UAC, which had gone into the correct position but wasn't sampling back. She pulled that back, having confirmed on the Xray that it had gone in too far, and it started sampling when placed at 9 centimetres. So the gas that's documented before is an arterial gas rather than a capillary gas, which gives us a much more accurate evaluation of the situation and in fact that gas is completely acceptable: normal pH of 7.34, normal CO2, and a base excess which would be acceptable, and a normal lactate. A normal lactate would mean that in fact perfusion was adequate.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Just so we understand, what's the significance of the arterial sample?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So you're sampling more centrally, if you like. When you take a capillary gas you can't fully evaluate the oxygen content of the blood because the blood has gone out to the capillaries by then, whereas an arterial gas gives you a very accurate measure of exactly what's going on.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right, okay. We can then see, if we scroll down a little, reference to X-rays or an X-ray.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Explain those to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. She's then commented that the UAC is probably actually a UVC and is in the liver, which we wouldn't want to happen. So she's pulled it back further. So actually, that gas is probably a venous gas rather than an arterial gas.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But it's still acceptable and in fact as a venous gas is a good gas.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right. Do you recall during that conversation what [Baby D]'s breathing status or ventilation status was at that stage in the afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know without there being a record.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: If you don't remember, you don't remember. Could I ask next for tile 136.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we go to the fluid balance chart, please. If we can look at the entry, please, at 1.30 that afternoon on the right-hand side (inaudible).
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it is, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We can zoom in, I think, if that helps.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's fine. So a fluid bolus has been given.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And the purpose of the fluid bolus?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: To help with tissue perfusion.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. There we go.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Lovely.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We can see there a little more clearly an entry at 13.30, "Saline bolus, 0.9%" is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: And volume, 30ml?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Initialled by the nurse on the right-hand column?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Did you have any more conversations or contact with [Baby D] during the course of the rest of that particular afternoon or evening?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I recall, no.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We've heard that [Baby D] had an episode at about 1.30 in the morning, so into the Monday when you would still have been on call.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Do you remember that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Can you tell us what you remember of that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I remember Dr Brunton phoning me to say that [Baby D] had had an episode of profound desaturation and he asked if I would come and have a look and go into the hospital and assess her.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Okay. Any particular reason he wanted you to come and have a look that you can recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't... I mean...
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We can go to your notes in a minute. I wonder if you can remember.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A baby that had -- you know, I think it was because she had been so stable and then had deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: If we can go to slide 218, please. If we scroll down a little bit, please, we can see Dr Brunton's signature on the left.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We can see -- and we've been through this already so I'm not going to ask you about this. We can see his notes that he made. We can see the last line that he wrote in his manuscript was:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Discussed with Dr Newby. Will R/V [I assume] on NNU."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Will review", yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: We can scroll down then. That's your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: If you could read that for a moment, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
I would like you just to talk us through that entry, please.
Okay. So I arrived on the unit around 2 in the morning.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: It was just that she was going off and she said that the other two are in there, you should be okay, but just in case, just to keep a listen out. It wasn't a formal arrangement, it was just to keep an eye out. I remember I went in to look at the baby, she was nice and stable and settled. I just checked around all the monitoring and everything that she was stable and then I left the room.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Is that something you would routinely do when you were asked to cover a break?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I tend to, yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: So you actually went into room 1, you satisfied yourself as to firstly [Baby D]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: I should ask you, who was the baby? That's my mistake.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And you satisfied yourself as to her condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: You checked the equipment, I think you said?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Well, I checked the monitoring and her saturations and her heart rate were okay.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: You told us you then felt able to leave the room at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Do you remember what time that was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was round... Round about half 12, 00.20, something like that, or even 1 o'clock. I'm not really sure what time that was at the time.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: All right. What happened after you'd left the room?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The baby seemed quite settled. I popped in another time, about 10 minutes later, and she was okay. I was at the desk round the corner because of having the other babies, I was trying to keep a listen out for my other babies.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Let's just pause there because I think we've still got the plan up on the screen. Can you give us an idea of where you're describing when you were at the computer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was round the corridor.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: If we look at the plan we can see rooms 2, 3 and 4 up the left-hand side.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: We can see a corridor running up almost the centre up to the left and nursery 1 to the right. Perhaps using the numbers or any of the rooms that have a name, can you give us an idea where it was close to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was between room 2 and room 3. It was actually...
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: It was a bit further round -- where is it? Where 5 is the milk room, it was before that, it was just round the corner, because there is another door on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: We have heard in fact, if we look at nursery 1, there are two doors into nursery 1. The second door is not marked, it should be to the left there as we look. Are you saying it was closer to there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: So you were there, you were keeping an ear out for your respective babies. Tell us what happened then, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was aware that alarms had gone off, so I don't know whether somebody had shouted me or that it was the alarms that alerted me, but I went into the nursery.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Which nursery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Into nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Right. And what did you find in nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The baby, her monitoring was showing that she was desaturating and her heart rate had dropped.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Which baby, sorry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Baby [Baby D]. I wasn't -- I don't know whether there was anybody else around the baby at the time, but I think there might have been. I checked on the baby's condition. I'd quickly put some hand sanitiser on my hands and was going to go in to give the baby gentle stimulation and see if the baby needed any oxygen, see if the baby would recover from that.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: We've heard there's sort of a process when a baby desaturates --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: -- which is a staged process, would you agree?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: So you were going to begin by?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Gentle stimulation and check on the baby's head position, whether she'd put her chin on her chest. Had she -- was she breathing. That would alert whether we needed other means.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: You thought someone else might have been there in the room, you can't say for sure. Did you do this on your own or were you assisted by anybody?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think I was assisted by somebody.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Can you (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't clearly remember who it was, but I have a feeling it might have been Lucy, but I can't categorically say who it was.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Right. Let's concentrate on what you recall doing. Did the gentle stimulation work?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It did start to bring the heart rate up, but then the saturations still remained low, so we would give the baby some CPAP -- would give some -- use the Neopuff and put some oxygen and gave some facial oxygen and then would give some PEEP. And then the baby still wasn't really responding, so we would give some gentle breaths by the Neopuff, with putting the head in the right position so that you got a good airway.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember who used the Neopuff?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was me.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Right. Did [Baby D] respond to the Neopuff?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She did start to respond, but also in the process, the doctor was called. I don't know whether the doctor was in the room at the time, Dr Brunton, or he was -- or we actually called him in as well.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay. When you were tending to [Baby D] and with that gentle stimulation or during the Neopuff, did you notice anything about her?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know whether it was during or just after, but we noticed that she had some sort of -- there was a rash on her trunk and arms.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Right. Are you able to be a bit more specific about where it was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was on her body, her arms and her -- so all from her chest downwards, her trunk and her arms, and it wasn't like a normal rash that you would know if a baby was becoming septic because they tend to be -- the blood vessels seem to be more bluey and they're just quite mottled. This was more -- there seemed to be a larger -- like mosaic-type rash, and it was a reddy-blue -- reddy-brown colouring.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: All right. So not like the rash you might ordinarily see, is that what you're saying?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: What do you mean by a mosaic?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It wasn't like a petechiae, which is like a spotty rash, it was more like the vessels or like oval-type markings on the skin, but like the vessels of blood, or whatever it was, seemed to be meeting up on each other.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay. So oval in shape?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And were those vessels meeting up with each other forming that oval shape or is that something else?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's what it appeared to be, what I can recollect, yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay. And can you remember the colour of the rash, if we call it that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was quite a pale-skinned baby, so they seemed to be more pronounced and a browny-red.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Browny-red, okay. You mentioned it appeared to be blood vessels. Did you form a -- from your experience were you able to recognise it from anything you'd seen before?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not before, no. The only thing I could think of, the way it was, was some sort of like -- I've seen something, but I don't know whether it's before or after this, something where you get -- where the baby has discolouration on one side of the body, it's likes a harlequin discolouration. But really this is -- we hadn't actually ever seen anything like it before.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: So at the time you didn't feel you'd seen anything like it before?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Do I take it then that the other occasion you're describing with a harlequin-like appearance, that's since this particular incident?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Are you able to say roughly when that was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, no.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Are you able to say where it was when you saw it on the second occasion as in which place of work it was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was within Chester, yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay. You can't tell me how soon or long it was after this one?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, but that harlequin-type effect wasn't on [Baby D], it was on a subsequent baby (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: So different on the second baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: But obviously in your own mind you have linked the two?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I hadn't linked, I just -- I think I said to Dr Brunton, I said, "The only thing I can think of is", when we're trying to work out what this rash was, I said it's very -- how it came and went was like a harlequin sequence for other babies. That's the only thing. So I had seen it in a previous baby in my experience beforehand, but not -- that was — it was just trying to come up with a solution why this baby had done this.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: You said you discussed it with Dr Brunton; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: At what time? Can we just be clear? When did you discuss it with Dr Brunton, at the time you saw it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, it was at the time, and it was later discussed when Dr Newby came in as well.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: We're concentrating on that first occasion when you are describing the rash to us and you discussed it then with Dr Brunton?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay. Tell us, please, what happened as things then proceeded.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then as much as I'm aware, [Baby D] then responded and her breathing returned and she settled back into a normal pattern of breathing.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay. Are you able to -- do you recall how long that might have taken, for example?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't, no, I'm afraid. It was a bit of a blur.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: I understand that. Did you notice what happened with the discolouration?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After a while, that seemed to disappear and dissipate.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay. Did you see [Baby D] again during the course of the remainder of your shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not aware that I did, but I might have been called in at other times in the subsequent events later on.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: But I was probably busy outside with the babies that I had.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: So when these incidents take place, does everybody rush to the same place or are there other responsibilities ongoing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There are other responsibilities and because of the staffing that was in the room and if there were other people available, they would deal with that.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But I would have always gone in and seen if they needed any assistance if I was able to.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Right, okay. Do you have any recollection of doing that or any other significant events involving [Baby D] that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure. I might have helped with drawing up some drugs or trying to find things for people, but I'm not aware of what I did.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Thank you. I have no more questions. If you could wait there.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
My Lord, I'm asked to ask one additional question if I may.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly, of course.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If we can go to tile 12, please. This is a document, as you may have seen, entitled "Blood gas record", from the intensive care unit at Chester. If we can scroll down, please. You'll be familiar with these sort of forms, I take it, and the entries thereon?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Could I ask you to look, please, at an entry at 01.14, which is a little further down. Bearing in mind what you told us about the timings that morning, can you tell us whether that is your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, that's not my handwriting.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: All right. Thank you. My apologies for that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
I'm just going to ask you a couple of general questions and then just a few points about the incident you've told us about.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You'd worked, by the time we're dealing with, at the Countess of Chester for about 20 years, hadn't you, something like that?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: You noticed, didn't you, that between June 2015 and July 2016, which is the period we're looking at in this case, it did seem to be a particularly busy period, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Did you form the impression at least that there seemed to be a lot of sick babies who were admitted?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There were a lot of babies that became sick, yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Well, I'm helped by the statement -- you made a statement to the police, didn't you, on 9 January 2018 --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: -- after you'd been interviewed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And what you described is that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "During this time we were particularly busy and a lot of sick babies were admitted."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's what --
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Does that help jog your recollection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: All right. You were used to the way that the unit operated and the sort of babies you normally had admitted, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And one of the things that struck you was that it seemed to you that some of the babies who came were babies who would normally have been born at other hospitals?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There was a hope that you could transfer some babies out, yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: A hope that you could?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Because it seemed that some of the babies that you had seemed to be the sort of babies who would normally be in a tertiary unit, wouldn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There were changes made, yes, so they were to take certain levels of babies, yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: That who was to take them, sorry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The tertiary hospitals would take them.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: But wasn't the impression that you had that some of the babies who you had at Chester were babies who normally would have expected to be at the tertiary unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When we were extremely busy, yes, some of them should have been at that tertiary units, but unfortunately those tertiary units were busy also.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: That's what I wanted to establish, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can I just ask you something else, again it's a general point. If your attention is drawn to a baby who you've identified as unwell in some way or possibly becoming unwell, for instance if there's an alarm or you just noticed they're desaturating, in the first instance in your experience does a nurse take time just to confirm what the problem is before they act?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And then you would take whatever action you thought necessary to deal with the problem once you've assessed what it is?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Is it the case that there are obviously levels that you can respond and sometimes you might wait just to see if the baby self-corrects?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: If that doesn't appear to be happening and if you believe you can, you might then react by stimulating the baby or even giving the baby some oxygen yourself?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's correct.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And then if the problem seems to require more assistance then you'd ask for assistance from another nurse; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Or you might even crash call a doctor if it's something which looks more serious?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: When we look at the events for [Baby D] on the 21st and 22 June 2015, did you find, when you cast your mind back to them, that a lot of details were not clear, some may have been and some were not?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm sorry, I'm unsure.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Did you rely a lot on notes and things like that that you'd read to help you with recalling details?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did, yes. That's what I had to look at.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: All right. You became aware that [Baby D] had desaturated; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was alerted.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Alerted, right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Would it be right, you're not too sure what it was that drew your attention to that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. I'm unsure whether it was the alarms or it was somebody shouting for help.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: We know that Caroline Oakley, whose nurse [Baby D] was, came back from a break --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: -- to assist. Do you recall asking Lucy, Lucy Letby, to go and fetch her at some point during what happened, that is Lucy Letby to fetch Caroline Oakley?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know who I was asked to go and get Caroline but we asked -- we said, "Can you go and get Caroline please".
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Your recollection, tell me if this is right, is that one or other of you went to get Caroline?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: But you're not sure who it was?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: The discolouration that you've described to us, today you described it as a mosaic, red/brown colour, and you have said things to the jury that it was like vessels, oval markings and she was pale and it was a browny-red. That's what you said in evidence now.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When you described this to the police -- I am looking at the statement on 9 January 2018 which is a couple of years after this, about 4 years ago from now -- at that time what you said was that [Baby D] had been mottled over her trunk and legs.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And then you just said that you'd seen babies in the past with discolouration from circulation issues or from sepsis, but on this occasion it looked unusual.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And that's actually as much as you said back in 2018 about the colour.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Right. You made this statement after being interviewed by the police, didn't you --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: -- as a witness.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: No reference to mosaic or reddy-brown or vessels or things like that, was there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: I just wonder if you could help us. That extra detail, is that something that you may have picked up from what other people have said when you've gone back and talked about this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I might have done, but also it's my recollection. There are other elements that have come back that I remember and thinking -- because it was so unusual.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: I'm not disputing you said it was unusual, but you accept that it's possible that you may have been influenced a bit by discussions that have talked about the colour of the rash?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It... No, because it was an odd rash. It wasn't like a normal septic rash. It was a different type of rash.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: But when you gave the statement to the police and you were interviewed, you were able to give as much detail as you could remember, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And you had the time to do that, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And can you help us with why you didn't provide, for such an unusual rash, details like mosaic, red-brown vessels then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because when I was asked, I wasn't -- I couldn't actually describe it, I just said it was very unusual and it was like a mottled-type rash, which would -- it was still a mottled rash but it was unusual.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: People have talked about this rash amongst work colleagues, haven't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm. I think -- I'm not... Not that I'm aware of.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Can you help us with how you got the extra detail?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because I started thinking about what happened in the events because I was -- as I was getting sleepless nights, I was thinking about the events that happened.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: But certainly not something you remembered or are able to describe when you actually made the statement after the interview 4 years ago?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not at the time, no.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Sorry, the date of that statement?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 9 January 2018.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We can agree that all you said about it then, Ms Percival- Calderbank, is that it looked unusual?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: In any event, you went on to say that the discolouration disappeared and she became a normal colour again?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: And, as far as you could tell at that point, she seemed to have recovered from whatever it was that had taken place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: PERCIVAL-CALDERBANK

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All right. Well, by reference to your report, please, and we can go to the chart and point these things out one by one if we need to, do we start with [Baby D]'s heart rate at the top of --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- the chart?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And how did you -- how would you describe what we can see on that heart record, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. That is a normal heart rate record. The values vary all within the normal limits. There is one spike, ie increase in heart rate, just before the end of the mark, which then falls. So therefore a normal heart rate, apart from that one increased spike, which is around -- between 1 and 2 am. So therefore that's a normal heart rate apart from that one blip.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What about the respiratory rate, the respirations?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Same again. All the respiratory markers are within the normal range, they're all 40 to 60, and you get an increase to 60 around the same time as the increased heart rate. So you've
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: got two values of 60 and then you have the drop. So therefore normal respiratory pattern up until about 1 in the morning.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the temperature, any significance to any of those readings?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Normal temperature readings.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Further down the chart, if we could just scroll down, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think I'll open up my own because I can see it a bit better.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can we see [Baby D]'s blood pressure recorded there under BP?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause). Right, I'll check my own because I can't read that on there.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There's a blood pressure value of -- two blood pressure values. The first is 69/45 with a mean pressure of 53.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the next one is 66/34, with a mean pressure of 45.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the last one is 68/39, with a mean blood pressure of 48. All those values are perfectly acceptable for a baby of [Baby D]'s size and age. So normal in other words.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the other bits down the bottom, slightly above the value of BP, you can see O2 on the far left. There's a value O2. If you look at the values towards the right, there are three values of 21. There's 21, 21 and 21. That means 21% oxygen, of air, and underneath the line O2 you can see SaO2, that's what that reads, not very clear, it's oxygen saturation. There are three values: one is 100, one is 94, and the last one is 99.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So that relates to oxygen saturation and values of 94, 99 and 100. Perfectly normal, indicating good respiratory results.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. All right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So a very stable baby, in other words.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So [Baby D] in air?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: No supplemental or additional oxygen and recording blood saturations which, as you have told us, are perfectly acceptable?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you move on to consider the findings at the post-mortem?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you defer to the pathologist, Dr Marnerides, so far as the post-mortem is concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I do.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you consider the issue of the failure to give [Mother of Baby D] any antibiotics in the light of her premature membrane rupture?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did. I did -- I'm not sure. Yes. Yes, I did. Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I -- yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And I think to be fair, you also took into account the witness statement of [Mother of Baby D], which was supplied to you by the police, setting out the chronology of her treatment?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That is your paragraphs 30 and 31.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You recorded, I think at your paragraph 31, that [Baby D] had been born 60 hours after her mother's membranes had ruptured.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you flag up under your observations a need to clarify the hospital's policy regarding giving antibiotics to mothers in [Mother of Baby D]'s position following the early rupture of membranes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you consider -- I'm going to your paragraph 33 now, please, Dr Evans. Did you consider the Apgar scores at 5 and 10 minutes that had been recorded for [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. They were 8 and 9, which is -- both of which are satisfactory, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you also then -- I'm going to your paragraph 34 -did you also then look to seek to explain why it was that [Baby D] had been in a poor condition following her birth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. I thought that her condition was consistent with early onset pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And what features of [Baby D]'s condition caused you to reach that conclusion?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, she was -- the Apgar scores were satisfactory, so that's not too bad. But she was grunting and cyanosed soon after she was born and her respiratory rate was increased, so all of these are markers of some kind of respiratory problem.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the commonest respiratory problem in any baby of 37 weeks' gestation is infection, pneumonia. To add to that, her bilirubin was 92, which is raised, and although babies commonly get jaundice, if the bilirubin is abnormally high initially in the first 24 hours, it's not normal and in cases of infection the red blood cells haemolyse, they burst, and that causes the jaundice. So a raised bilirubin is a non-specific marker of infection in a situation of this nature. And on top of that, we've got grunting, which is again a well-recognised clinical indicator of something abnormal and worrying respiratory-wise. And of course she was cyanosed, you know, her colour was blue, was not normal.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So all of this, very straightforward, all of these added up to early onset pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you take the view that once she had been admitted to the neonatal unit, [Baby D]'s management had been acceptable or not?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Once she got there -- she was about 4 hours of age when she got there and I thought her management was entirely consistent with what I'd expect of a modern neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: She received antibiotics and she received respiratory support and intravenous fluids.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Was the decision to remove the ET tube from [Baby D] at about 9 o'clock on the morning of the 21st a reasonable one in all the circumstances?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was, because she was getting better. She was making what I consider a very satisfactory improvement -- and in fact a far more rapid improvement than I would expect given the condition she was in when she arrived at the unit. But all the respiratory markers, monitoring, that were carried out were great and therefore she was taken off endotracheal intubation, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Having removed the ET tube and the blood gas results that were then reported, was it a reasonable decision to put [Baby D] on to CPAP to support her breathing?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it was. Although she was satisfactory when full ventilation was removed, her condition did not settle completely and therefore standard management -- she still needs a little bit of support, CPAP is that form of support, so she was put on CPAP and she stabilised very, very promptly on what is, by any standards, very minimal respiratory support. So that was great.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And over the day, as we've heard, her condition stabilised and, you know, she remained very well.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Looking at things in the round and taking into account the evidence that appears in the records, and indeed that you have heard, what view did you come to so far as [Baby D]'s condition immediately prior to her collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can I just put one bit there to get the chronology right --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- if that's okay?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was stable on CPAP and the medical staff, in the evening prior to her collapse, took her off CPAP. This didn't work, so they put her back on CPAP. That is perfectly standard management, especially in a baby who by this time was not needing additional oxygen. She was a big baby, over 3 kg. Some babies don't like CPAP very much, you know, it's quite
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: intrusive, can be -- having something over your face. So they tried her off CPAP.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Her oxygen saturations dropped so they put her back on CPAP and her condition reverted to normal more or less straightaway and stayed perfectly normal in air, oxygen saturations normal, until the early hours of the following morning.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So what conclusion did you come to so far as her condition in the time immediately before her collapse some time after 01.00 hours on the 22nd?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just prior to that, if I'd seen her I would be very, very confident that she'd be very well the following morning and we would be looking to either maintaining her on CPAP, because she's still only, you know, a couple of days of age, or trying her off CPAP again to see if she can now breathe without CPAP.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So her condition could not have been better and her condition clinically was entirely consistent with a baby recovering from early onset pneumonia -- not recovered from pneumonia, recovering from pneumonia. Nobody, I think, recovers from pneumonia in such a short time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So this -- you know, she was really doing exceptionally well and clinically very satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: How would you describe [Baby D]'s response to the treatment that she had received?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When now?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In the time immediately before her collapse.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh, extremely satisfactory. You know, her improvement was far quicker than I would have expected, to be frank.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It was remarkable that her oxygen values -- oxygen saturations, you know, 100% or 99% without the need for any supplemental oxygen at all. Now, that is an indicator of a baby whose lungs are functioning satisfactorily.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So very good.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you having told us that there is clear evidence that her lungs were operating satisfactorily --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- can we look at the three collapses at about 01.30, 03.00 and 03.45 hours on the morning of 22 June, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We have heard evidence as to the nature of [Baby D]'s response following the first collapse. Is that typical in these circumstances?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It isn't, actually. It's very unusual because her deterioration was very rapid. Her oxygen fell, her heart rate fell. It was very rapid, which usually is an indicator of some kind of serious pathology, you know, but if it is an indicator of serious pathology, then resuscitation will work, but this is followed by the need for far more in the way of clinical support. In other words, she would need additional oxygen, she would not have recovered so promptly.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But within a very short period of time, she was back, not requiring oxygen, and well. So this is an incredibly unusual response for a baby who's 37 weeks' gestation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So what you're saying is the speed of her response and the nature of her response is inconsistent with the gravity of the collapse being part of the pneumonia that no doubt she had?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's inconsistent with the pneumonia or any other one of the -- inconsistent with what we call septicaemia or sepsis, in other words a generalised infection. If she had a generalised infection, sepsis, she would not have made this very prompt recovery within a very short period of time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Looking at your paragraph 39, Dr Evans, did you remark on the abdominal discolouration which had been reported by the treating medical staff?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The word I used was "intrigued". This was something that I found very unusual again. It was intriguing, both with regard to its appearance, and I think we've heard from the local people, local staff looking after her, their descriptions of all of this, noting tracking, bruises.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The other thing, which is even more remarkable, is that it disappeared. It disappeared within 35 minutes according to my report.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So these abnormalities, they could not be bruises.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think some of the treating doctors have referred to this, but why can't they be bruises?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Bruising is due to damage to blood vessels under the skin, whether you get kicked in the shins playing football or whatever. If you get damage to tissues underneath the skin, the blood vessels are traumatised, they break. Blood leaks out of the tissues and then comes close to the surface, where the bruise appears.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If that happens, as is the experience of all of us, I suspect, the bruising will last several days. So bruising will not disappear within a matter of an hour or two or less. So therefore this could not be bruises.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The other thing it could not be is what I think Dr Newby this morning described as purpura. Purpura, again, are blood spots. Same principle: tiny blood spots under the skin, which you get in any number of conditions. I think one of the people mentioned meningococcal septicaemia.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If you get purpura, if you get these little blood spots under the skin, they just don't disappear, they'll be there for days, and if they are due to some serious underlying condition, they don't just not disappear, but you get an increase in the number of purpuric spots. So you get a spreading of purpura and this is associated with continued deterioration in your baby, in your patient.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore the fact of all of this discolouration disappeared in a short time, not bruises, not purpura.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay. In coming to your final conclusion, which we will come to in a moment, did you note the report of the post-mortem X-ray that had been taken of [Baby D]'s body?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you ask for some assistance from a pathologist in terms of interpreting air which was found within [Baby D]'s body following her death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. We can leave that for them.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we turn to your opinion, finally, please, Dr Evans, so your paragraph 43. Dealing with the issue of pneumonia, first of all, so far as you could tell, was this a pneumonia that affected both lungs or one lung?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, the post-mortem says right-sided pneumonia, so just the right lung.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. In your experience, what conclusion did you draw as to when [Baby D] had developed pneumonia?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think she had developed it before her birth and that would be the result of the prolonged ruptured membranes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So this was an antepartum pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Antepartum, is that Latin for before birth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, before birth.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Lawyers aren't allowed to use Latin anymore. I don't think doctors are prevented.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as that was concerned, if [Baby D]'s pneumonia had been sufficient to cause her death, what would you have expected the pattern of her decline towards death to have been? How would that have presented?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sure. If a baby's born with a severe pneumonia, usually affecting both sides, but not necessarily, where treatment fails to save her, what you find is that increasing amount of clinical input does not lead to an improvement. I'll explain all of this.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When she first presented, she was an unwell baby and required ventilatory support. She was on ventilation, she wasn't on just this CPAP. If her pneumonia had progressed, the clinical team would never have managed to get her off ventilatory support and they probably would have found that as the hours went by, she would have required more and more oxygen, in other words a greater concentration of oxygen probably. She'd have required ventilation with increased pressures, in other words it would have taken greater pressure to keep the lungs open. They would have had difficulties keeping her oxygen saturations at a satisfactory level.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This is what you get in babies who have a severe or a fulminant pneumonia. In [Baby D]'s case, none of this happened. She got better. And as I've said earlier, she improved far, far more rapidly than I would have expected. I would have expected her to improve over 2 or 3 days, say, but she in fact improved over 24 hours -- or less than that, less than that, because she was placed on ventilatory support around 8 pm, I think, 9 pm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Intubated 9 pm, extubated 9 am.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And extubated 9 am. So over that night her improvement was such that she did not need what I would call full
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: ventilatory support anymore, which is great. On top of that, her oxygen requirements had fallen, you know, didn't need any, and so all of the prognostic factors, all of the predictions for [Baby D] at this time were she was recovering from pneumonia -not recovered, not fully recovered, but recovering from pneumonia and it would be therefore a matter of, and I use these words advisedly, a little bit of trial and error as to when the medical team would get her away from CPAP to get her breathing on her own.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So by 9 am -- at 10 am she was put back on CPAP and was stable on CPAP. So by any account, she was recovering satisfactorily from her pneumonia and essentially she was out of danger.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you exclude pneumonia as being the cause of [Baby D]'s death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no, the pneumonia did not -- was not responsible in any way for [Baby D]'s death. Pneumonia is probably the condition that clinicians like myself have dealt with more commonly than any other condition, you know, any other condition, really. And in a situation like this, you know, pneumonia with the correct treatment is curable. You just treat it, antibiotics, oxygen, breathing support if necessary, so standard pneumonia treatment. That's what we do. That's why she was in the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you reach a conclusion as to what had caused or what was consistent with being the cause of [Baby D]'s death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. As we know, as with when I've given evidence before, initially all I had to go on were the clinical records and I formed the view this is an extraordinarily unusual collapse, unexpected collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This is something that is consistent with her having sustained intravenous air. In other words, she'd received an injection of air, of gas, through a vein into her circulation, causing what we call an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As I've discussed earlier, air embolus is incredibly rare, but this is what -- this, I concluded, was the only explanation that -- the only cause that could explain [Baby D]'s collapse and death.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Those are all the questions I have for you. Thank you, Dr Evans. Would you wait there for some further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Evans, you haven't been asked, so I'll ask you, what are the features that make air embolism the only explanation?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right, well, let me go through them. The first is that her collapse -- this was a collapse of a baby who was stable and who had an intravenous line in place and where the collapse was unexpected and the changes were rapid and very, very striking. In other words -- the drop in oxygen saturation being the main one. So that was my first stage in reaching this diagnosis of air embolus.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The second stage was the presence of this discolouration, which is unique in two ways. The first is that it was a pattern of discolouration that experienced neonatal nurses had never seen before and experienced medical people, one of whom is now a neonatologist in Glasgow, had never seen before and had never seen since. So we've got this extraordinarily unusual pattern of discolouration.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The second aspect of the discolouration was that it came and it went. It came and it went. Again, this is something that you do not find as a result of sepsis or other disorders. So that was my second step.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: My third stage in reaching this diagnosis was that resuscitation was unsuccessful. This is the fourth of our 17 cases and I think we'll find in future cases that babies did deteriorate as a result of the usual complications that one gets in babies, infection mainly, and resuscitation carried out by experienced medical staff works. You don't need -- they just get better.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore the third step in getting to my diagnosis was the fact that she failed to respond to pretty -- well, pretty thorough efforts at resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: My fourth stage, which again I defer to the radiology and pathology opinion on, is the presentation of air in the great vessels. The local report said air in the aorta -- so the great vessels could be the aorta or the vena cava. So again we've got air in a great vessel, which is an incredibly unusual phenomenon, as our radiology colleagues will tell us. So that was stage 4.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The fifth stage is that none of the other issues that affected [Baby D] were relevant. You can't explain this on the presence of a pneumonia affecting one lung.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Her sodium was a little bit on the low side, you know, that wouldn't explain her collapse or discolouration or anything else. So therefore, putting -- so we have four stages followed by the fifth and I think have excluded everything else.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So in my opinion, in [Baby D]'s case, we had a full house of clinical characteristics entirely consistent with her having sustained an air embolus, ie air injected into her circulation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right, thank you. We'll come back to that shortly.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I want to go through next what we have in terms of her condition, leading up to the events in the morning of 22 June, Dr Evans --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think we might just have our mid-afternoon break at the moment.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, of course.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I was going to have to interrupt you at some stage.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think this is a good time to have it. We'll just have our 10minute break now. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

Mr Myers.

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It does.
blocks.speaker: EVANS
